To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

consonants and vowels are differentially involved in language processing, and that this difference is already present in the first year of life. The key words that characterize our work are "speech perception," "speech production," "language acquisition," "consonants," "vowels," and "phonetic learning."

(1) infants are sensitive to the functional differences between vowels and consonants; (2) vowels are more important than consonants in extracting and generalizing the structure of speech; (3) vowels are less important than consonants for identifying words; (4) these results suggest that infants are able from an early age to assign basic speech categories to different learning mechanisms, which may sustain early language acquisition
